item.title: Bangladesh First: A Nation Cannot Rise Unless Justice Reaches Everyone. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
When we say “Bangladesh First,” we are making a promise that this country, our country, will place the wellbeing of ordinary citizens above every competing interest. It is an emotional phrase, and rightly so, because after more than fifty years of independence, the question of what truly comes first for the average Bangladeshi remains deeply important.
Ask a farmer waiting years for a land dispute to be resolved. Ask a small trader who has spent his savings fighting a case he never expected to face. Ask a mother whose son spent months in custody before the charge against him was found to lack sufficient basis. Their answer to “what comes first” may not be economic growth figures or infrastructure projects. Their answer may be one word: justice. Justice that arrives on time, treats people with dignity, and does not exhaust a person’s spirit in the process of proving their innocence.
This is the conversation this anniversary piece hopes to open. Not about politics. Not about any single institution, party, or individual. It is about something broader and urgent: the importance of strengthening public trust in our legal and justice processes, and what delay, unequal access, and weak accountability can cost the quiet, law-abiding majority.
The Silent Majority Pays the Price
There is a particular unfairness when ordinary people struggle to access timely justice. It rarely appears as one dramatic event. Instead, it can happen through delay, repeated paperwork, procedural complexity, limited access to quality legal support, and informal practices that may benefit those with greater resources or networks.
The people most affected are often not the wealthy or well-connected. They may have options, legal support, and the patience that comes with resources. The people most affected are usually ordinary citizens: shopkeepers, farmers, garment workers, students, retirees, and families who believe that if they have done nothing wrong, the system will eventually recognize that.
For many, justice may eventually come, but only after years of hearings, adjournments, and legal expenses that quietly weaken a family. A case that should take months may stretch into years. A hearing that should be routine may take much longer than expected. During that time, a business can collapse, children’s education can suffer, health can deteriorate from stress, and even when a person is cleared, social stigma may remain.
This is the invisible cost that slow and uneven legal processes place on the public. It is not only financial. It is also emotional, psychological, and social. A person who has been wrongly accused, delayed, or detained does not simply move on once the paperwork says they are free. The experience can leave behind anxiety, fear of authority, and a lasting doubt about whether truth alone is enough. When repeated across many families, this becomes more than a legal issue. It becomes a social trust issue, and even a public wellbeing issue.
Weak Accountability Is a Shared Challenge
It would be easy, but not helpful, to point fingers at one office, one department, or one group of people. The real picture is more complex. Weaknesses in a legal and judicial ecosystem are rarely created by one actor alone. They can grow wherever oversight is limited, accountability is inconsistent, and systems allow delay or discretion to affect people differently.
This can happen at many levels: when files move slowly, when citizens do not know how to navigate procedures, when evidence is not handled efficiently, when delay becomes a strategy, or when influence appears to matter more than merit. The powerful can often afford delay. The powerless often cannot.
None of this is unique to Bangladesh. Many countries, both developing and developed, continue to wrestle with delays, access gaps, and public trust challenges in their justice systems. What matters is not blaming any single group, but recognizing the pattern honestly enough to improve it.
The concern here is not any person or political side. The concern is a culture where shortcuts become normal, truth becomes negotiable, and ordinary citizens carry the cost of systemic weakness. If Bangladesh truly wants to come first, then integrity, fairness, and accountability must come first as well.
“Bangladesh First” Must Begin with Honesty First
There is a reason the words “Bangladesh First” resonate so strongly. They suggest a reordering of priorities, a decision to place the collective good above narrow interests, shortcuts, and convenient silence. But this cannot happen through slogans alone.
It requires an honest national commitment to a simple truth: a country cannot develop faster than its ability to deliver justice fairly. Roads, bridges, digital systems, and economic growth matter. But for a citizen caught in a long and uncertain legal process, development also means the confidence that truth will be heard, procedures will be fair, and dignity will be protected.
If we are serious about putting Bangladesh first, we must also put truth first, timeliness first, and equal treatment under law first, regardless of who is seeking justice and who is being asked to answer for their actions.
A nation that protects integrity in its justice processes protects not only courts and laws, but also the confidence of its people.
Building the Culture We Want, Starting from the Classroom
If integrity is not only a legal issue but also a cultural one, then the solution must also begin early. Laws can be amended, systems can be digitized, and courts can become more efficient. These steps are necessary. But they will not be enough if the next generation grows up believing that dishonesty and shortcuts are simply “how things are done.”
This is where education can play a larger role. Many students learn about the Constitution, fundamental rights, and government structures as exam-oriented facts. What is often missing is a practical understanding of civic ethics: what fairness means, why truth matters, how false accusations harm real people, why bribery weakens society, and why due process is not a burden but a protection for everyone.
This understanding cannot come from one textbook chapter alone. It should be woven into education through lessons on honesty, justice, empathy, and responsibility. Schools and universities can use debates on ethics, mock court activities, storytelling, drama, community service, and real-life case discussions to help students understand the human cost of injustice. When young people practice fairness rather than only memorize it, honesty becomes a habit, not an inconvenience.
Imagine a generation of Bangladeshis who grow up understanding that a lie told for short-term gain can damage another person’s life for years. That generation would not need integrity to be forced upon them. They would already see it as part of who they are.
A Happy, Safe Bangladesh Is the Goal Itself
At the heart of this conversation is a simple idea: people want to live without fear. Fear of being falsely implicated. Fear of losing years to a case that should have been resolved earlier. Fear of seeing an honest complaint delayed because the process feels too slow, too expensive, or too difficult to navigate.
A “happy Bangladesh” is not measured only by GDP charts or skyline photographs. It is also measured by whether an ordinary citizen can sleep peacefully knowing that if they are wronged, the system will treat them with dignity and seriousness.
A “safe Bangladesh” is not only about physical security. It is also about legal security: the confidence that truth matters, that due process works, and that no one’s future will be harmed simply because they lack power, money, or connections.
This is what “Bangladesh First” should mean: a country that chooses to strengthen justice before celebrating progress too loudly. A country that teaches its children early that honesty is strength, not weakness. A country that understands that every shortcut, every delay, and every failure of fairness quietly reduces public trust.
The ordinary people of this country, those who work, pay taxes, follow rules, wait patiently, and still try to believe in the system, deserve better than delay, fear, and uncertainty. They deserve a legal and justice system that heals rather than harms, protects rather than punishes the innocent, and moves with the urgency that justice requires.
If Bangladesh truly wants to come first, it must begin with a difficult but necessary commitment: to build not only more roads, buildings, and institutions, but also stronger habits of honesty, fairness, and trust. Only then can we say, without hesitation, that we have put our people, happy, safe, and justly treated, first.
The views expressed in this submission are personal and reflect a broader civic concern for institutional reform, not directed at any individual, group, or organization.
